sceneFacts.shortVersion: Michelin chef rated film's star pursuit 9/10 for accuracy.
sceneFacts.longDescription: Michelin-starred chef Paul Liebrandt reviewed fine-dining scenes from "Burnt" for Insider. He noted that common beliefs about Michelin inspector criteria, such as ordering a tasting menu or arriving early, were "hearsay." Liebrandt emphasized that Michelin inspectors primarily look for consistency in all aspects of the dining experience. He ultimately rated the film's depiction of the pursuit of Michelin stars as a near-perfect 9 out of 10 for accuracy.

sceneFacts.shortVersion: Real chefs were extras in the film's kitchen.
sceneFacts.longDescription: To ensure authenticity, Lupt Utama served as the Assistant Costume Supervisor for "Burnt." The film's kitchen set was built as a fully functioning kitchen, designed to work like a real restaurant. Real chefs were cast in minor roles in the cooking scenes, adding to the realism for the actors. Consultant chef Marcus Wareing even turned the stoves on full during filming to make the actors hot and sweaty.

sceneFacts.shortVersion: Alicia Vikander's role was added to the script at Harvey Weinstein's request.
sceneFacts.longDescription: Alicia Vikander portrays Anne Marie, the ex-girlfriend of Adam Jones and daughter of his former boss. Her character's role was not initially part of the script. The part was specifically added at the request of Harvey Weinstein.

sceneFacts.shortVersion: The Langham Hotel in London was a key filming location.
sceneFacts.longDescription: The film features a fine dining restaurant located at The Langham Hotel in London, specifically The Roux at the Landau. This restaurant appears throughout the film, and its dining room was staffed with at least 24 people working on the service side at any one time. Some of the extras in the film's kitchen and restaurant scenes were genuine chefs, adding to the authenticity.

sceneFacts.shortVersion: Bradley Cooper and Sienna Miller cooked in a real, hot kitchen.
sceneFacts.longDescription: To create an authentic, high-pressure kitchen environment, the film's set was a fully functioning kitchen, designed to operate like a real restaurant. Consultant chef Marcus Wareing trained Bradley Cooper and Sienna Miller to genuinely cook and act like professional chefs. During filming, all food preparation was done for real, with actual chefs as extras, and Wareing even turned the stoves on full to make the actors hot and sweaty, enhancing the intense realism of their performances.

sceneFacts.shortVersion: Chef Marcus Wareing ensured kitchen scenes were authentic.
sceneFacts.longDescription: Michelin-starred chef Marcus Wareing consulted on the film for seven years, starting with script development. His role included designing the kitchen set, creating menus, and training the actors to cook. Wareing ensured all food preparation was done for real, even turning up the heat on set to make the actors look like genuine chefs.

sceneFacts.shortVersion: The film was originally titled 'Chef' but had to change.
sceneFacts.longDescription: The film was initially intended to be titled "Chef", but this name was already claimed by a Jon Favreau movie. Pre-sales for this film, then called "Chef", occurred at Cannes simultaneously with Jon Favreau's "Chef" picture. Sony, who originally set up the project, issued a cease and desist letter regarding the competing title. Producers then considered "Adam Jones" as a title before ultimately deciding on "Burnt".

sceneFacts.shortVersion: Burnt's opening weekend was among the lowest on record.
sceneFacts.longDescription: Released in 3,003 theaters on October 30, 2015, "Burnt" pulled in just over $5 million during its opening weekend. This made it the fourth worst opening on record for a film playing in over 3,000 theaters. Despite this initial low performance, the film eventually managed to earn back its $20 million budget within a month of its release.
